prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- London commuters crammed onto buses, scrambled for taxis, cycled or simply walked on Wednesday as a strike by Tube workers shut down most of the subway network. Commuters queue for packed buses in London on Wednesday morning. The strike began Tuesday at 7 p.m. (2 p.m. ET) but the first full effects were felt during Wednesday's morning commute. The strike was set to last for 48 hours with a normal service resuming Friday morning, according to Transport for London (TfL), which runs the city's transportation network. The RMT trade union called the strike after talks with management over pay, job cuts, and disciplinary issues broke down. "RMT doesn't resort to industrial action lightly," General Secretary Bob Crow said in a statement. "The fact is that Tube workers have been driven into walking out today." Transport Commissioner Peter Hardy said the talks had been making progress on all issues and he urged the RMT to return to the table. "The RMT leadership says we were close to a deal," Hardy said in a statement. "If that is the case, then they should call off the strike, return to talks ... and resolve this issue without any more disruption to Londoners." TfL was running extra buses and free shuttle services across the River Thames during the strike. Electronic travel cards used for the TfL network were temporarily being allowed on all train lines in greater London, it said. While most services on the Tube were shut because of the strike, one line -- the Northern line -- was running normally and five others were running on a reduced schedule, TfL said. "It's been really good," a girl on Oxford Street told CNN about her commute. "The Northern line is running perfectly." Still, some bus services were packed with commuters who normally ride the underground trains or who failed to find a taxi. "I think we'd all like to strike for more money, but unfortunately we can't," said one woman at Oxford Circus, where the Tube is closed. Others hit the pavement and walked. "It's OK -- quite refreshing," said a man on Regent Street. He said he had just walked from Liverpool Street Station, a train station as well as a Tube stop that is more than 2.5 miles away. The RMT represents about half of the 20,000 employees on the Tube, a TfL spokeswoman said. Other unions including Unite and TSSA represent the rest, she said, and were not on strike.

**LONDON, England (CNN) —** London commuters crowded onto buses, scrambled for taxis, cycled, or simply walked on Wednesday after a strike by Tube workers shut down most of the subway network.

Commuters queued for packed buses across London on Wednesday morning. Although the strike began Tuesday at 7 p.m. (2 p.m. ET), its full impact was first felt during Wednesday’s morning commute.

The strike was scheduled to last 48 hours, with normal service expected to resume Friday morning, according to Transport for London (TfL), which operates the city’s transportation network.

The RMT trade union called the strike after talks with management over pay, job cuts, and disciplinary issues broke down.

“RMT doesn’t resort to industrial action lightly,” General Secretary Bob Crow said in a statement. “The fact is that Tube workers have been driven into walking out today.”

Transport Commissioner Peter Hardy said progress had been made on all issues and urged the RMT to return to the negotiating table.

“The RMT leadership says we were close to a deal,” Hardy said in a statement. “If that is the case, then they should call off the strike, return to talks ... and resolve this issue without any more disruption to Londoners.”

During the strike, TfL operated additional buses and free shuttle services across the River Thames. It also temporarily allowed electronic travel cards used on the TfL network to be accepted on all train lines in Greater London.

Although most Tube services were suspended because of the strike, one route—the Northern line—was operating normally, while five others were running on reduced schedules, TfL said.

“It’s been really good,” a girl on Oxford Street told CNN of her commute. “The Northern line is running perfectly.”

Nevertheless, some bus services were packed with commuters who would normally travel by Underground or who had been unable to find a taxi.

“I think we’d all like to strike for more money, but unfortunately we can’t,” said one woman at Oxford Circus, where the Tube station was closed.

Others took to the pavement and walked.

“It’s OK—quite refreshing,” said a man on Regent Street. He said he had just walked from Liverpool Street Station, both a railway station and a Tube stop more than 2.5 miles away.

The RMT represents about half of the Tube’s 20,000 employees, a TfL spokeswoman said. Other unions, including Unite and TSSA, represent the remaining workers and were not participating in the strike, she added.
outputs.L2:
LONDON, England (CNN) — A walkout by London Underground employees brought most of the Tube system to a halt Wednesday, forcing travelers to squeeze onto crowded buses, compete for taxis, ride bicycles or make their journeys on foot.

Although the strike started at 7 p.m. Tuesday in London—2 p.m. Eastern Time—its full impact became apparent during Wednesday morning’s rush hour, when passengers formed lines for packed buses. Transport for London (TfL), which operates the capital’s transit network, said the stoppage was expected to continue for 48 hours, with regular service returning Friday morning.

The RMT union organized the industrial action after negotiations with management collapsed over wages, proposed job losses and disciplinary matters.

In a statement, RMT General Secretary Bob Crow said the union did not take strike action casually, adding that Underground employees had been pushed to the point of leaving their jobs that day.

Transport Commissioner Peter Hardy maintained that discussions had been advancing on every disputed issue and called on RMT officials to resume negotiations. In a statement, Hardy noted that the union’s leadership had said an agreement was near. If so, he argued, it should end the walkout, return to the negotiating table and settle the dispute without causing London residents further inconvenience.

To ease the disruption, TfL deployed additional buses and operated free shuttle services across the River Thames. It also temporarily permitted electronic TfL travel cards to be used on every rail line throughout greater London.

Despite the closure of most Underground services, the Northern line continued to operate normally, while five other lines offered limited service, according to TfL.

One girl interviewed by CNN on Oxford Street described her journey as very good and said the Northern line was working perfectly.

Elsewhere, buses were overwhelmed by passengers who would ordinarily use the Tube or who had been unable to secure a taxi. At Oxford Circus, where the Underground station was closed, one woman remarked that everyone would probably like to strike for higher pay, but most people did not have that option.

Some travelers chose to walk instead. A man on Regent Street called the experience acceptable and “quite refreshing.” He said he had walked from Liverpool Street Station, which serves both mainline trains and the Tube and is located more than 2.5 miles away.

A TfL spokeswoman said the RMT represents roughly half of the Underground’s 20,000 workers. The remaining employees are represented by other unions, including Unite and the TSSA, neither of which was participating in the strike.

counterfactuals.output:
# 48-hour London Underground strike brings widespread disruption across capital

**London** — Millions of commuters faced crowded buses, soaring demand for taxis and longer journeys by bicycle and on foot as a 48-hour strike brought much of the London Underground network to a standstill.

The walkout disrupted services across the capital, leaving many stations closed and forcing passengers to seek alternative routes to work, school and appointments.

Long lines formed at bus stops during the morning rush hour, while traffic slowed on several major roads as more people turned to cars and taxis. Ride-hailing users also reported limited availability and higher fares in some areas.

Others opted for two wheels, with cyclists filling routes through central London and rental bikes in high demand near major transport hubs. Crowds of pedestrians streamed across bridges and along busy streets as commuters completed all or part of their journeys on foot.

Transport officials advised passengers to allow extra time, avoid peak periods where possible and check services before traveling. Some rail and bus connections remained operational, but increased passenger numbers placed pressure on the wider network.

The strike was called amid a dispute involving working conditions, staffing and proposed changes to Underground operations. Union representatives said the action was necessary after negotiations failed to produce an agreement, while transport authorities warned that the shutdown would cause significant disruption.

Businesses across central London also felt the impact. Some employees worked from home, while shops, restaurants and offices reported delayed arrivals and reduced foot traffic.

Emergency and accessibility arrangements remained a concern throughout the walkout, particularly for passengers unable to cycle or travel long distances on foot.

Normal service was expected to resume gradually after the 48-hour action ended, though officials cautioned that delays could continue as trains and staff returned to scheduled operations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the Tube workers’ strike in London, explaining when it began, why the RMT called it, how Transport for London responded, and how commuters were affected.
counterfactuals.output:
### London Underground strike — 15 March 2023

A 24-hour strike by London Underground workers began shortly after midnight on **Wednesday, 15 March 2023**, bringing almost the entire Tube network to a halt.

The **RMT union** called the walkout over concerns about planned reductions in staffing, possible changes to employees’ pensions, and alterations to working conditions and agreements. It said Transport for London’s financial plans—developed after government funding settlements—could lead to around **600 station jobs being lost** and undermine safety and working practices.

**Transport for London (TfL)** said it was seeking savings because of its financial position but maintained that staffing reductions would largely be achieved by not replacing workers who left, rather than through compulsory redundancies. TfL also said it had not put forward a specific proposal to change pensions and urged the unions to continue negotiations.

The strike caused severe disruption for commuters:

- Most Underground lines had **little or no service**.
- Buses, the Elizabeth line, London Overground and National Rail services became substantially busier.
- Roads were more congested, while many passengers walked, cycled or worked from home.
- Some disruption continued into the following morning as trains and staff returned to their normal positions.

The action coincided with the UK government’s Budget Day, increasing its visibility and adding pressure on TfL and ministers to resolve the dispute.

**Fictional breaking-news report**

# Most of London Underground to shut after pay and job-cut talks collapse

**LONDON, Wednesday** — Most of the London Underground network is expected to shut down after negotiations over pay, proposed job cuts and disciplinary procedures collapsed late Tuesday, union and transport officials said.

The walkout is due to begin overnight, with severe disruption expected throughout Wednesday and into Thursday morning. Transport for London warned passengers that only limited services may operate and urged them to work from home, walk or cycle where possible.

Union leaders said management had failed to provide sufficient guarantees on staffing levels, wages and the handling of disciplinary cases.

“Our members will not accept declining real-terms pay, fewer frontline staff and a disciplinary system they believe is being used unfairly,” a union spokesperson said. “We remained ready to negotiate, but the revised offer did not address the central issues.”

TfL said it had made a “fair and affordable” proposal and accused the union of rejecting measures intended to modernize the network.

“We are deeply disappointed that talks have ended without an agreement,” a TfL official said. “The action will cause major disruption to millions of passengers and to London’s economy. Our door remains open, and we urge union representatives to return to discussions.”

National Rail and Elizabeth line services are expected to continue, although stations that also depend on Underground staff could close at short notice. Buses are likely to be far busier than usual, with long queues anticipated during the morning rush hour.

Commuters reacted with frustration as warnings appeared at stations Tuesday evening.

“I have two changes to get to work, and there really isn’t a practical alternative,” said Hannah Reed, a hospital administrator from north London. “I understand why staff are worried about jobs, but passengers are always the ones caught in the middle.”

Daniel Okoro, who works in retail in the West End, said he planned to leave home nearly two hours early. “I can’t work remotely, so I’ll have to take three buses,” he said. “If they’re full, I don’t know what I’m supposed to do.”

Further talks have not yet been scheduled. TfL advised passengers to check live travel information before beginning their journeys.

counterfactuals.output:
**London commuters face widespread disruption as RMT strike shuts Tube network**

**LONDON, 15 March 2023** — London commuters faced severe travel disruption on Wednesday as members of the Rail, Maritime and Transport union staged a 24-hour strike across the London Underground.

Transport for London said **no Tube lines remained operational during the main part of the walkout**, with services suspended across all 11 Underground lines. Stations were closed or left without enough staff to operate safely, and passengers were warned that disruption could continue into the following morning as trains and employees returned to position.

The stoppage involved RMT members working in a range of operational roles, including station staff and train operators. The union said it represented **more than 10,000 workers across London Underground**, and called the strike amid disputes over pensions, staffing levels, working conditions and proposed changes linked to TfL’s financial plans.

Although the Underground was shut, other parts of London’s transport network continued to operate. Passengers were advised to use the **Elizabeth line, London Overground, Docklands Light Railway and London Trams**, none of which forms part of the Tube network, although some services and stations were busier than usual.

TfL also deployed additional buses where possible, but warned that the capital’s roads and bus routes were likely to be heavily congested. Travellers turned to **National Rail services, Santander hire bicycles, river boats, walking and cycling** as alternatives. Taxis and private-hire vehicles were also in greater demand, while long queues developed at several major transport hubs.

The Elizabeth line provided an important east–west alternative, but central London interchange stations experienced crowding. Some stations served jointly by Underground and other rail services had restricted access because Tube staff were unavailable or because passenger numbers became too high.

Commuters were urged to allow extra time, check live service information before leaving and avoid travelling at the busiest periods. TfL cautioned that replacement transport could not match the capacity of the Underground, which normally carries millions of passengers on a weekday.

The RMT said the industrial action was intended to protect jobs, pensions and existing employment agreements. TfL, meanwhile, said it was seeking reforms needed to place its finances on a sustainable footing and called on the union to continue negotiations.

Businesses in central London reported delayed staff arrivals and reduced footfall, while many employers encouraged workers to operate from home. Schools, hospitals and other public services also advised employees and visitors to plan alternative journeys.

Even after the formal end of the strike, passengers were told to expect a gradual rather than immediate return to normal, with early services the next day potentially delayed or cancelled.
